name: Betaza Zapotec, BZ
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

MA report, University of Texas at Austin. x+197 pp. Open copy: CORE mirror of the UT Austin repository,https://core.ac.uk/download/10646629.pdf(Glottolog ref 318074, filed under cajo1238).
catalog_locator: Chapter 8 'Stress', section 8.1 'Stress in native words', pp. 175-180; section 8.2 loanwords pp. 180-182; conclusions p. 187; vowel length non-contrastive: p. 93 and section 6.1 p. 131.
catalog_quote: In BZ, monosyllabic words are stressed on the roots with long vowels and short vowels if they are content words. ... Particles and prefixes of the form CV are normally unstressed. ... When the unstressed forms are added to a content root or stem, the root maintains the primary stress and the suffix or particle bears secondary stress. ... The roots or stems always maintain their stress, as shown in (192), and a secondary stress occurs on the affixes. ... In disyllabic words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, and the syllable can have low, falling, and occasionally high tone. ... I conclude that vowel length is the determining factor on the forms listed in (193a-f). Vowel length attracts the primary stress on the penultimate syllable. For the forms with high tone in (193g-i), I posit that in the sequence of two light syllables, the primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable. ... In polysyllabic forms, primary stress tends to fall on the ultimate syllable, and the secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. ... I conclude that primary stress placement is associated with vowel length: length determines stress. ... In disyllabic roots with low and high tone, the first syllable has primary stress if it is a content word; the second syllable, normally an affix, has secondary stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Cajonos Zapotec (cajo1238) is not in the catalog. The single stress-titled item, Teodocio Olivares 2009 (MA report, UT Austin; Glottolog files it under zad as 'Betaza'), was already held by the project with a text and was read in full for Chapter 8: it is a first-hand, instrumentally supported description of the San Melchor Betaza variety and states that stress is root-bound and length-driven (root/penultimate primary stress in native disyllables, initial in two-light-syllable roots, final in 3+-syllable words and long-final compounds, Spanish loans keep source stress), with the author calling it preliminary. No catalog record exists to confirm or contradict. The only Cajonos-proper stress statement known (Nellis & Hollenbach 1980, IJAL, reported second-hand by Teodocio as root-initial stress) remains paywalled (doi:10.1086/465639, uchicago 403) and is the high-priority acquisition.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress sits on the root/stem: monosyllabic content words are stressed, CV prefixes and particles are unstressed, and suffixes/clitics added to a root carry only secondary stress, so disyllabic (root+affix or disyllabic-root) words are stressed on the penult = root-initial syllable. The author ties placement to vowel length: a long (low/falling-tone) syllable attracts primary stress, so low+falling compounds and tri-/polysyllabic words have primary stress on the long final syllable with secondary stress on the penult; two light syllables default to initial. Spanish loans keep the source stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Affixes and clitics attached to a root bear secondary stress (root keeps primary); in compounds and polysyllabic words with final primary stress, secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds with low+falling tone and polysyllabic words stress the (long) final syllable rather than the penult; prefix+root disyllables are final-stressed because the root keeps stress; CV particles/prefixes unstressed; loanwords (old and recent) retain the Spanish stressed syllable, even when reduced to monosyllables; stress is not marked in the practical orthography; tone is contrastive (H, L, falling, rising) and only partially correlated with stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (field data, Praat); language is tonal with four contrastive tones, stress described as independent of tone in monosyllables and partially correlated (low/falling, longer vowels) in disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Zapotec of San Melchor Betaza (Villa Alta district), which the author classes as a Xhon-group dialect alongside the Cajonos towns, Yaganiza, Yalalag, Zoogocho etc; Glottolog 5.1 files this thesis under cajo1238 (Cajonos Zapotec, iso zad), but it is not San Pedro Cajonos or San Pablo Yaganiza proper. For Cajonos proper the primary phonology is Nellis & Hollenbach 1980 (IJAL), not opened here; Teodocio reports it second-hand as root-initial stress. The thesis notes tonal inventories differ between Betaza (H, L, falling, rising) and San Pedro Cajonos (four tones incl. mid).

new_statements.reading: Betaza (Xhon/Cajonos-group) Zapotec has root-bound, weight-sensitive stress: content roots carry primary stress and CV affixes/particles secondary or none; in root+suffix disyllables stress is root-initial (penultimate), a long or falling-tone heavy syllable attracts primary stress wherever it sits (so many compounds are final-stressed), two-light-syllable roots default to initial stress, and words of three or more syllables take primary stress on the final syllable; Spanish loans keep their source stress. Not a fixed-position system; the closest catalog's classification would be weight-sensitive (vowel length) with a root-initial default, and the author flags the analysis as preliminary. Variety caveat: San Melchor Betaza, not San Pedro Cajonos/Yaganiza.

tone_statements.citation: Cruz Vargas, Sandy. 2020. Las oraciones de complemento en el zapoteco de San Miguel Cajonos. Tesis de maestria (Maestria en Linguistica Indoamericana), Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropologia Social (CIESAS), Ciudad de Mexico. Director: Oscar Lopez Nicolas. (febrero 2020; repository deposit 2020-12-13).
tone_statements.quote: Por su parte, el sistema tonal en esta variedad de zapoteco consta de tres tonos fonológicos, dos tonos nivel, el tono bajo /B/ y el tono alto /A/, y un tono de contorno, el tono descendente /AB/. Todas las vocales fonológicas de la lengua, con independencia de su cualidad modal o no modal, pueden expresar el tono; sin embargo, las vocales no modales resultan de particular interés por el hecho de combinar, en un mismo segmento vocálico, dos gestos articulatoriamente contradictorios: la tensión transversal de las cuerdas vocales para la expresión de los diferentes grados de laringización y la tensión longitudinal de las cuerdas vocales para la expresión de los contrastes tonales ...
tone_statements.translation: The tonal system of this Zapotec variety consists of three phonological tones: two level tones, low /B/ and high /A/, and one contour tone, falling /AB/. All phonological vowels of the language, whether modal or non-modal, can carry tone; the non-modal vowels are of particular interest because they combine, in a single vocalic segment, two articulatorily contradictory gestures: transverse tension of the vocal folds for the degrees of laryngealisation and longitudinal tension for the tonal contrasts ...
tone_statements.locator: p. 41, section 2.2.2 'Sistema vocalico y sistema tonal' (pp. 40-42), ch. 2; tone diacritics also in 'Abreviaturas' front matter and section 2.2.3
tone_statements.summary: Three phonological tones: level Low, level High, contour Falling (High-Low); tone-bearing unit the vowel/syllable nucleus (all 12 vowel phonemes, modal and laryngealised, bear tone); tone interacts with non-modal phonation ('complejidad laringea').
